tagline: Riverbank cobblestones, a pike village and a minister’s six-sided study
intro: Wellsburg stands along the Ohio River; east of town, Fowlerstown lies on West Virginia Route 27. Near Bethany, Alexander Campbell’s house stands on Route 67, with its outbuildings north of the road and the family cemetery to the south.

The public wharf at Wellsburg was built in 1836. Along Washington Pike, Fowlerstown grew at William Fowler’s grist mill. In Bethany, minister Alexander Campbell founded a college in 1840, then laid out the town in 1847.
Begin with Wellsburg’s surviving wharf cobblestones, then turn to Fowlerstown’s brick Greek Revival inn. At the Bethany end, Campbell’s house has a small hexagonal stone library nearby.

moments.title: Wellsburg Wharf
moments.text: Cobblestones along the Ohio River bank mark the remains of Wellsburg’s public wharf, built in 1836. The site also contains the foundations of two warehouses, one built by Danforth Brown. The wharf entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
moments.notice: Look for riverbank cobblestones and the foundations of two warehouses.

moments.title: Fowlerstown
moments.text: Fowlerstown grew along Washington Pike at William Fowler’s grist mill. Its historic inn, also called Drover’s Inn, was built between 1848 and 1851 as a two-and-a-half-story brick building in the Greek Revival style. Before 1938, it housed the village’s general store and post office. A two-story log house from 1820 and a frame cottage on the property both predate the inn.

moments.title: Alexander Campbell Mansion
moments.text: Alexander Campbell’s house grew to accommodate both teaching and visitors. John Brown built its central portion in 1793; Campbell married Brown’s daughter Margaret in the parlor in 1811. In 1819, Campbell enclosed the west porch and added a second story for seminary dormitories. An addition in 1836–40 accommodated visitors. Beside the enlarged house stands the small hexagonal stone building he used as his library and office. Campbell founded Bethany College in 1840 and served as its president until his death. The college now cares for the house, which became a National Historic Landmark in 1994.
